newsitem.title: INDIA: New plants seen hurting Asian petrochem prices.
newsitem.headline: New plants seen hurting Asian petrochem prices.

text.p: Plans for more petrochemical plants in Asia threaten to depress prices and profit margins in 1997 and 1998, analysts said on Wednesday.
"We are negative on the industry for two years," said an analyst at a leading U.S. investment bank.
He said large plants being built in China, Thailand and India would outstrip growing demand in the region.
The bank estimates annual ethylene capacity in China will grow to 4,065,000 tonnes in 1997 from 3,960,000 tonnes in 1996.
Ethylene, produced from naphtha or natural gas, is the building block for petrochemicals.
India's ethylene capacity is expected to jump to 1.7 million tonnes this year from 574,000 tonnes in 1996.
Two major operations, a 700,000-tonne-a-year plant of Reliance Industries and a 300,000-tonne plant of the state-run Gas Authority of India, are to be commissioned in calendar 1997, analysts said.
Reliance's ethylene cracker, India's largest, is expected to start production within a month, they said.
Thailand is also building large plants. Ethylene capacity in Thailand is expected to touch one million tonnes a year in 1997 from 751,000 in 1996, according to the U.S. firm.
Nandini Krishnaswamy, analyst at Caspian Research in Bombay, said the average earnings of Indian petrochemical firms were expected to fall in 1996/97 (April-March).
"Net earnings are projected to decline 5.6 percent on the back of the downturn in the petrochemical cycle...," she said.
"The domestic market for all major polymers will move towards surplus capacity by 1997/98, opening up export possibilities," said Peregrine Capital in a January report.
While exports will help absorb excess capacity, margins will be compressed, the report said.

An analyst at securities firm James Capel B&K said the new local plants were all built to the minimum economic size of 300,000 tonnes of ethylene a year. "The demand does not pick up so fast," he said.
Said an analyst at an Indian broking firm: "Petrochemical prices are a little firm now, but are expected to fall."
Prices of raw materials such as naphtha have been rising with firming crude oil prices in recent months. This would lead to a squeeze on producers' margins in the next two years.
"Demand should begin to catch up (with supplies) by 1999," said an analyst. "Until then, the picture is bleak."
"I see price wars," said a broker. He said Reliance Industries had cut polyethylene prices in January and other Indian producers might have to follow soon.
He expected an upswing only in 1999/2000 (April-March).
